senses: A pair of tight-fitting trousers, worn by men and women in South Asia.
ety: From Punjabi ਚੂੜੀਦਾਰ (cūṛīdār).

senses: Sentimental, emotional.
ety: Shortened from sentimental.

senses: African cornmeal porridge
ety: Borrowed from Swahili ugali, from an Eastern Sudanic language.
examples: Still tall as the doorway, still fat from crocodile meat and ugali porridge.

senses: The stationary part of a motor or other machine.
ety: From stationary or static by analogy with rotor; alternatively from a hypothetical Latin stātor (literally “stander”); all ultimately from stāre (“to stand”).

senses: The first downy hairs that appear on the chin.
ety: Via Latin pappus from Ancient Greek πάππος (páppos), an affectionate term for elderly men (referencing beards).

senses: The social context one inhabits that shapes and defines a person's identity and perspective.
ety: From positional + -ity.
examples: In the post-civil rights era, some white men have adopted a marginalized positionality in an effort to reclaim the tacit social privileges of being white, heterosexual and male.

senses: A person who poisons something or someone.
A cook working in the outback.
ety: From Middle English poysener; equivalent to poison + -er.
examples: A station ‘poisoner’ in his own kitchen is a dictator indeed.

senses: That which perceives.
ety: Borrowed from Latin perceptor.

senses: A cotton fabric with a short pile, resembling velvet.
ety: From velvet + -een. Compare veloutine, from French.

senses: A person who works in, or is an expert in, parasitology.
ety: From parasitology + -ist.

senses: best, A1, superior.
ety: From top + flight.

senses: A dark form of soy sauce.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 醤油 (shōyu). Doublet of soy.

senses: Toward the tail end (hind end) of the body; in bipeds such as humans, this direction corresponds to inferior.
ety: Borrowed from Latin caudālis (“having a tail”).

senses: An aquatic plant, Hydrilla verticillata
ety: From the genus name Hydrilla.

senses: The process of being, or state of having been, made liquid (from either a solid or a gas).
The liquid or semiliquid that results from this process.
ety: From Middle English liquefaction, from Middle French liquefaction (modern French liquéfaction), from Medieval Latin liquefactiō.
examples: Whenas in silks my Julia goes, / Then, then (methinks) how sweetly flows / That liquefaction of her clothes.
Where we might usually have applied dressings and put bandages on, many people weren't able to keep dressings on their cats clean and dry because houses and gardens were full of liquefaction.
The student army carried on shovelling liquefaction and the women in the homes nearby fed them without a thought.

senses: Resembling or characteristic of lemons, especially in terms of aroma, taste or colour.
ety: From lemon + -y.
examples: The walls were painted a lemony yellow colour.
We were served a lemony cheesecake for dessert.

senses: An explosive low-pitched sound resembling a burp.
ety: Imitative; compare burp, bleep, etc.
examples: It would start, then stall, then start again with a blurp, while clouds of blue smoke and sickening gas fumes polluted the air.

senses: An alewife (type of fish).
ety: From French gaspereau, a variant of gaspareau.

senses: A small document, included with an employee's wage or salary, giving details of income earned and tax and insurance paid.
ety: From pay + slip.

senses: (of an official or feudal lord) Having local authority and possessing royal privileges that elsewhere belongs only to a sovereign.
Subject to palatine authority. (of a territory)
Synonym of palatial.
ety: From late Middle English palatyne, from Old French palatin, from Medieval Latin palātīnus (“relating to the palace”), from palātium (“palace”) + -īnus (“-ine”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of paladin.

senses: Shaped like a boat.
ety: From Latin scaphoides, from Ancient Greek σκᾰφοειδής (skăphoeidḗs, “like a bowl, hollow”), from σκᾰ́φη (skắphē, “boat, trough, bowl”).

senses: A chiropractor.
Chiropractic.
ety: Shortening of chiropractor, chiropractic.

senses: The process of categorizing something (e.g. history) into named periods.
ety: From period + -ization.

senses: Having the quality of adrenaline or epinephrine.
Containing or releasing adrenaline.
Activated by an adrenal mechanism.
ety: From adren- + -ergic.

senses: A male red grouse.
ety: From moor + cock.

senses: A traditional Mexican soup, made from hominy, pork, chilli and other ingredients.
ety: From Spanish pozole, from Classical Nahuatl pozolli (“stew of maize kernels”).

senses: A follower of neofascism.
ety: From neo- + fascist.
examples: By this summer, everything — her youthful admiration for Benito Mussolini, her party’s links to neofascists, her often extreme rhetoric — had been forgiven.

senses: Percina caprodes, an American freshwater fish, the log perch, rockfish, a kind of darter.
A large, red, spiny-headed, European marine fish (Scorpaena scrofa).
A pinfish, Lagodon rhomboides, ranging from Massachusetts to Texas.
A grunt, Haemulon parra.
ety: From hog + fish.

senses: The extent to which something is communal.
ety: From communal + -ity; compare earlier commonalty, commonality.

senses: Characteristic of a spindle; slender and of weak appearance.
ety: From spindle + -y.

senses: A deep-fried burrito
ety: From Mexican Spanish chimichanga (“trinket, thingamajig”), but the original sense is disputed and obscure. See chimichanga.

senses: An ancient book of the Roman Catholic Church, containing the rites for Mass, the sacraments, etc.
ety: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin sacramentarium; compare French sacramentaire.

senses: Gimmicks collectively.
The use of gimmicks.
ety: From gimmick + -ry.

senses: A member of the religious police in Saudi Arabia.
The religious police as a body.
ety: From the Arabic مُطَوَّع (muṭawwaʕ, “compliance officer, pious volunteer”), from طَوَّعَ (ṭawwaʕa, “to subjugate”).

senses: The rank or post of a chancellor.
The office or staff of a chancellor.
The building in which such an office is situated.
ety: From Middle English chancelrie, from Old French chancelerie (Modern French chancellerie), from Late Latin cancellaria. Doublet of chancery.

senses: especially Atriplex hortensis
or Atriplex patula, found in dry habitats, that have edible leaves resembling spinach.
ety: From Middle English arage, from Anglo-Norman arace, arache; apparently an irregular derivation from Old French arepe, from classical Latin atriplex, from Ancient Greek ἀτράφαξυς (atráphaxus), of unknown origin (probably loaned).

senses: The act of scarifying: raking the ground harshly to remove weeds, etc.
A medieval form of penance in which the skin was damaged with a knife or hot iron.
The scratching, etching, burning / branding, or superficially cutting designs, pictures, or words into the skin as a permanent body modification.
ety: From Old French scarificacion, from Late Latin scarificatio. See scarify for more.

senses: A type of traditional Japanese comedic storytelling.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 落語 (rakugo).

senses: A variation in the volume of a note or a chord, evoking a tremor or quiver.
The device in an organ that produces a tremolo effect.
ety: Borrowed from Italian tremolo, first-person present indicative of tremolare (“to shake, to tremble”). Origin: 1715-25.

senses: Surrounding, or traveling around the Moon
ety: From circum- + lunar.
